en: Volume Two, Part Two.
Composed by Li Tongxuan of the Great Tang at Beiping.
Third: The Dwelling of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-vihāra*). Here, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is primary, with the other nine as its companions. [Southern Meaning]
As stated previously:

"Traveling sixty yojanas south from here" clarifies that after completing the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, one again contemplates the active conceptualizations manifest upon the six sense faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and becomes fully liberated from all active conceptualizations within each individual faculty.
Previously, through the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, one cultivated wisdom by observing the three factors of the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness.

Now, in this stage, because wisdom follows the functioning of the six sense bases and there is nothing that is not liberated through discernment, it is said: "From here, travel south for sixty yojanas."

Regarding the path to Laṅkā: this Mount Laṅkā is situated in the midst of the great ocean, surrounded on all sides by the vast sea. The mountain is steep and lofty, with no gates or entrances on its flanks; it is difficult to approach and difficult to ascend.

Upon this great seashore there is a path; by clarifying the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), one reaches the Great Path and transcends birth and death.
By clarifying the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), one establishes the realm of wisdom; with neither faculty nor object stained, one transcends the ocean of birth and death.
This serves to represent that the mountain is difficult to approach and difficult to ascend, yet now it has been successfully climbed; hence it is called the "Lankā Path."

Because a bhikṣu practices walking meditation in mid-air like Mount Laṅkā, he attains entry from the void by clarifying the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*). Through the arising of the three dharmas of wisdom, one realizes that the great ocean of ignorance and birth-and-death, and the high mountains of self-conceit (*māna*), hatred, and delusion, are exceedingly difficult to transcend. Now, through the power of skillful means in the contemplation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one understands that the faculties, objects, and consciousness are all entirely empty. Ignorance is extinguished, the ocean of birth-and-death is dried up, and the high mountains of self-conceit are shattered. Wisdom purifies the six sensory dusts like the full moon; therefore, it is said that by the side of the path of Laṅkā, there is a village named Seashore (*Sāgara-tīra*).

Now that the six sense faculties have all become the ocean of wisdom, the five aggregates, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the objects of the six sense faculties are collectively the great ocean of the dharma-realm and the mass of universal radiance wisdom.

When Sudhana arrived at the coastal village of Laṅkāmārga, he surveyed the ten directions in search of the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita. He again contemplated the habitual tendencies within his own six sense faculties, causing them to accord with the principle of emptiness; furthermore, he observed that the objects within the six sense faculties of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were collectively of one nature—empty space—and thereby caused their seeing, hearing, sensing, and touching to become empty.
The village of the dharma-realm traversed by the gateways of wisdom is such that all sounds, fragrances, sights, and sensations encountered therein are entirely the dharma-realm.
The bhikṣu named Well-Abiding is so called because he clearly abides in the emptiness of dharmas and constantly acts for the benefit of others, never departing from the emptiness of dharmas.

Because he comes and goes and performs his walking meditation within space, he is named "Well-Abiding" (Susthitamati); this clarifies that he constantly performs all practices within the ocean of birth and death.
Both the ocean of birth and death and his activities for the benefit of sentient beings are never apart from space, as they are free from any defilement.
Regarding the passage "Having been honored by the Heavenly Kings, the Dragon Kings, and the Ten Kings," there are two meanings:

first, it clarifies that one has attained the Way and thereby summoned [their respect]; second, it signifies that by practicing the ten *pāramitās*, one attains mastery like a king. These details are found extensively in the sūtra text.

Regarding the three spiritual friends mentioned above: first, the Bhikṣu Cloud of Virtue on the summit of Mount Wondrous Peak represents the initial stage where the marks [of conditioned phenomena] are exhausted; because his wisdom-light is lofty, supreme, and supramundane, he is represented by a bhikṣu.

The second was the bhikṣu Sāgaramegha from the country of Samudramukha. Having attained through his own realization the wisdom-light of the realm of all Buddhas, which is free from all marks, he contemplated the active functions of birth-and-death—the ocean of all self and others, the twelve links of dependent origination, the six sense faculties, name-and-form, and consciousness. Thereby, he established the great ocean of light of fundamental wisdom and attained the Dharma-door of the Universal Eye Sutra.

Third, at the coastal village by the side of the path to Laṅkā, there was the bhikṣu Supratiṣṭhita, who attained the bodhisattva liberation door of unimpeded swift offerings to all Buddhas and the maturation of sentient beings. By clearly and repeatedly contemplating the habitual tendencies of the six sense faculties, he attained the further shore of crossing the ocean of birth and death; he attained the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena and achieved the further shore of mastery over birth and death for the benefit of the world.

The three spiritual friends mentioned above clarify how one attains purity by eliminating the afflictions within the twelve links of existence and the six sense faculties among the five aggregates, thereby accomplishing the karma of supramundane wisdom and liberation.
The practice of solely delivering sentient beings remains a world-transcending achievement within the gateway of cultivating the path; such is the proper correspondence of affairs.
For this reason, it is represented by the bhikṣu, to clarify that the bhikṣu is one whose conduct transcends the mundane.
Therefore, when Sudhana reached this stage, he asked:
"How does one practice the Buddha-dharma?
How does one accumulate the Buddha-dharma?"
...up to: "How does one not abandon the vision of the Buddha, but instead constantly and diligently cultivate the bodhisattva path?
This is explained at length as stated in the sūtra.

By posing these paired questions regarding this stage, it is shown that the Buddha-dharma and the bodhisattva-dharma are harmoniously integrated, thereby clarifying the accomplishment of supramundane wisdom.

From the passage "The Bodhisattva’s worldly practices are not yet mastered" onwards, the intent clarifies that one does not depart from the fundamentally pure wisdom of the world while studying the worldly wisdom of a Bodhisattva.
From "Then he showed [him]" onwards, the lay spiritual friend Megha, who dwelt in a marketplace, taught the gateway of the Adornment of Wheel-Syllables.
Subsequently, the lay spiritual friends such as the elder Vimokṣaka and others demonstrated that the clamor of the world is itself liberation, without needing to dwell in mountains or empty spaces.

Shifting that preceding mind to bring it to completion in the subsequent stage—this refers to those who have already ascended, such as Megha, the Householder Vimokṣa, and the Bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja—who have accomplished the worldly while remaining inseparable from the supramundane; these represent both laypersons and bhikṣus.
The fourth stage, the Abiding in Noble Birth, takes the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*) as its primary quality, with the other nine as its companions.
The meaning of "South" is as explained previously.
There is a land named Darbhikā; this country is located within the borders of South India, and its name has not yet been translated [into Chinese].

As for the name of the city, "Sovereign" (Īśvara): because this spiritual friend has attained supramundane wisdom and is also thoroughly proficient in conventional truth, he possesses mastery over both the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—and thus the city is named "Sovereign."
Among them was one named Megha; he was a layman who lived in a marketplace and appeared in every way like an ordinary person, which is why he was called a "person.
Because he resided in a marketplace and could not be designated by the titles of "Elder" (Gṛhapati) or "Householder" (Kulika), he was simply called a "person."
Megha means "One Who Subdues All Erroneous Doctrines.
Thus, Megha asked Sudhana:
"Have you already resolved to attain bodhicitta?"
Sudhana replied, "Yes.

Megha descended from his seat, prostrated himself before Sudhana, and cast five limbs to the ground; he scattered flowers and offered immeasurable kinds of jewels and incense as an offering to Sudhana.
The subsequent teaching on the "Gate of the Adornment of the Wheel of Syllables" is intended to clarify the Bodhisattva’s reverence for the bodhicitta.

Because Sudhana has attained the light of the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom, and Megha dwells within that fundamental wisdom, this serves to clarify reverence for fundamental wisdom; it is because one reveres supramundane wisdom by means of mundane reverence.

To clarify that when a bodhisattva dwells in the world and practices the bodhisattva path, they neither emerge from nor sink into, nor are submerged within, the ocean of birth and death, and thereby attain an immeasurable ocean of merit—it is solely due to fundamental wisdom that this is so.
For this reason, those who attain this wisdom must revere it.

To clarify that it is the fundamental universal radiance of great wisdom—the source of all myriad virtues, the root for transcending birth and death, and the origin of those who practice great compassion; it is the palace, hall, and pavilion of Samantabhadra’s conduct, the mother who gives birth to all sentient beings, the clothing, food, and drink that nourish all sentient beings, and the great ocean of life-sustaining resources. Since the roots of goodness of humans and devas are all produced from this fundamental wisdom, it must be revered.
Therefore, upon hearing that someone has resolved their mind toward enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one regards them as a Buddha.

Thus, when Megha heard that Sudhana had already generated the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, scattered flowers, various incenses, and precious garments as offerings to Sudhana; having paid his respects with profound reverence, he then preached the Dharma.
This refers to Not-Disparaging (Adhimukta), who did not slight those who had not yet studied, but revered those who studied as if they were Buddhas.
He manifested light from his mouth for Sudhana to clarify the teaching.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Wheel-Syllable" (*Cakrākṣara-parivarta*) that he expounded for him: "Wheel" (*cakra*) signifies the meaning of perfection.

Teaching the Dharma by means of worldly names and designations, it is perfectly pure and capable of destroying all unwholesome karma of birth and death. Its phrasing, meaning, names, and explanations are complete in sequence; those who see, hear, receive, and uphold it attain the karmic activity of pure wisdom, which destroys the karma of birth and death, breaks the ocean of unwholesomeness to become a great ocean of goodness, and breaks the ocean of ignorance to become a great ocean of wisdom.
They shatter the ocean of poverty and suffering to become a great ocean of merit and virtue.
Each and every phrase and meaning is mutually perfected through the relationship of primary and attendant elements, never losing the intent of the Path.
The exposition of each and every phrase and meaning is like Indra’s net, with all parts interpenetrating one another.
Within each and every syllable, according to the capacities and faculties [of beings], immeasurable wheels of Dharma are turned.

Mundane names and dharmas are transformed so as to become dharmas that transcend birth and death; mundane dharmas can be transformed into Buddha-dharmas, mundane delusion can be transformed into wisdom, and mundane speech and sounds can be transformed into the speech and sounds of all Buddhas, extensively expounding immeasurable benefits.
To summarize and illustrate this, it can be seen through reflection:
from the passage "I only know this Dharma-gate of the Radiance of the Bodhisattva’s Wondrous Sound Dhāraṇī" onwards, this is the advancement through the promotion of virtues.

The fifth is the stage of being fully endowed with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-vihāra*). Here, the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine serve as its companions.
The meaning of "south" is as explained previously.
Proceeding south from here, there is a village named Vana-vāsin; at this stage, a kingdom or city is not mentioned.

However, proceeding south from here, it is clarified that while the marketplace is a place of clamor, Maitreya’s presence therein is tranquility; it is clarified that the dust and toil of the great ocean of birth-and-death for all sentient beings constitute the marketplace; and it is clarified that not departing from the clamorous place of worldly birth-and-death constitutes dwelling in the forest of dhyāna.
Regarding "village" (*grāma*): it is a place where many people dwell, and such a multitude constitutes a village.
This clarifies that the realm of birth and death is a place where sentient beings are numerous; yet for the wise, dwelling therein is a forest of meditation (*dhyāna-vana*).

The former was Megha and the present one is the householder Vimokṣaka; because they both regard the worldly clamor of birth and death as a state of tranquility, he travels southward—mentioning neither direction, nor country, nor city, but simply saying he travels south.
"South" signifies correctness; "traveling" signifies ascending progress. Because it constitutes the True Dharma and represents ascending progress, it is said that "from here one travels south.

Since all the mundane realms of birth and death and their dusty environments are collectively regarded as the village of the Dharma and collectively as the grove of meditation, it is said that he "dwells in the forest."
Because this fifth dhyāna-body takes the realm of all sentient beings as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it is represented by the lay follower, the Elder Vimukta.

He turned back the minds of the three previous bhikṣus that were directed toward the supramundane, causing them instead to enter the villages of birth and death among sentient beings as his "Village of the Forest of Dhyāna.

At the abode of the elder Vimokṣa, Sudhana requested the Dharma; the elder Vimokṣa, through the power of his own roots of goodness, the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, and the power of Mañjuśrī’s mindfulness, [taught him].
Because the essence of the wisdom-body of the Dharma is pure and inherently possessed by all, this is the power of one's own roots of goodness.
Because the fundamental wisdom is, from the beginning, eternally quiescent despite its great functions throughout the ten directions, this is the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
The self-purifying wisdom first revealed is that which can be initiated through the wisdom of emptiness of the signless Dharmakāya; this is the power of Mañjuśrī’s recollection.

Furthermore, taking this very fundamental wisdom of purity as the gateway to dhyāna, its nature is inherently stainless and all-encompassing, forming a single body in which all buddha-fields mutually contain one another, like reflections in light.

Furthermore, in each direction, there appeared as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten Buddha-lands, adorned with purity; their bodies were like clear lapis lazuli containing all reflected images, with physical forms unimpeded, manifesting within them the appearance of infinite Buddhas arising in the world and entering parinirvāṇa.

All Buddhas, sentient beings, the inexhaustible karmic fruits of the three periods of time, and all manifestations appear clearly because the nature of luminosity is stainless and the nature of dhyāna is inherently all-pervasive; there is no space it does not pervade, and no realm that does not contain it.

The fundamental nature of non-conditioned pure wisdom is itself thus the perfect law of cause and effect throughout the three periods of time; it is itself thus devoid of the nature of extension or contraction, and cannot be produced through effort.

This is the dhyāna of the self-nature of all worldly dharmas; since all realms are from the beginning inherently settled and inherently still, the householder Śreṣṭhidatta is used as a metaphor for this, so that one does not seek joy or attainment apart from the world.
A practitioner should have such faith and understanding and practice in this way: when the myriad phenomena of the world appear before them, they are all dwelling forests and all are dhyāna groves.
It is solely because worldly beings forcibly seize the realms of others that they cling to distinctions of right and wrong, and to their own lands versus those of others.
Their minds thereby give rise to various karmas, which will inevitably produce bitter fruits; knowing this, what else can one do?
From "Since I have only known this liberation gate of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Adornment" onwards is the advancement through the exaltation of virtues.

These two preceding sections clarify that the mundane essence is fundamentally true: the clamor of the world is itself stillness, and the nature of all myriad objects and the mental capacity of all sentient beings is inherently the gate of dhyāna.
The sixth stage, the Abiding in Rectified Mind, has the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as its primary element and the other nine perfections as its companions.

The description of traveling south from here to the edge of Jambudvīpa illustrates that, upon reaching this stage, one’s practice extends to the ultimate boundaries of both supramundane and mundane phenomena.
The three bhikṣus from Mount Sumeru downward represent supramundane wisdom and liberation.
From the elder Megha up to this Bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja represents mundane-supramundane wisdom and liberation; these are represented by two laymen and one bhikṣu.
There is a land named Mālikāra, which has not yet been translated [into Chinese]. Therein dwells a bhikṣu named Sāgaradhvaja.

Having accomplished this sixth path of Prajñā, his body, mind, thoughts, and perceptions are stilled and do not arise; he is free from inhalation and exhalation. From thirteen parts of his body, various transformation bodies emerge to benefit beings throughout the ten directions. His wisdom is like the ocean, and his body and mind are tranquil, entirely devoid of discursive thought; thus he is called "Dhvaja" (Banner).
Sudhana saw the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja sitting cross-legged beside the walking path, free from inhalation and exhalation.
The walking path represents activity, while sitting cross-legged and being free from inhalation and exhalation represents stillness; this illustrates the unimpeded nature of stillness and activity.

As for Your Reverence’s manifestation of countless hundreds of thousands of billions of assemblies of elders, householders, and brahmins who transform and benefit beings throughout the ten directions, this is to clarify that the conduct and dwelling of these elders, householders, and brahmins are humble and lowly; they are free from pride and do not exalt themselves. It is for this reason that Your Reverence manifests these assemblies of householders and brahmins.

The emergence from both knees of countless hundreds of thousands of billions of kṣatriyas and brāhmaṇas signifies that they belong to the royal caste; it clarifies that "knees" (jānu) carries the meaning of mastery over extension and contraction, and it clarifies that kings possess mastery over the world, just as bodhisattvas possess mastery over birth and death (saṃsāra).

Regarding the emergence from the waist of a multitude of sages equal in number to all sentient beings: this clarifies that the waist is the locus where the five desires are practiced, whereas the sages represent purity and detachment from the five desires.

This clarifies that although Bodhisattvas dwell within the realm of desire, they are never defiled by attachment; because they are neither attached nor detached, remaining eternally pure, this is symbolized by the rishis.

As for the emergence from both flanks of inconceivable hosts of nāgas and inconceivable hosts of nāga maidens who benefit sentient beings in the ten directions, this clarifies that the two flanks signify the meaning of supporting and providing shelter.
The great wisdom and compassionate mind are clarified by means of the dragon and the dragon maiden.
The dragon represents wisdom, and the dragon maiden represents compassion.
Like a Bodhisattva who constantly dwells within the emptiness of phenomena, wisdom and compassion are ever-pervasive; they sustain and shelter sentient beings by raining down the Dharma.

Regarding the appearance of countless hundreds of thousands of billions of asura bodies from within the svastika on the chest: the svastika on the chest is the character for "ten thousand" (wan), signifying that the Bodhisattva performs the ten thousand practices within the cycle of birth and death without perishing; this is symbolized by the asura king.
Because the Asura King dwells within the great ocean, his feet reach the seabed and the water reaches his waist.

From his back emerge countless hundreds of thousands of billions of followers of the Two Vehicles—śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Because those of the Two Vehicles turn their backs on saṃsāra and turn their backs on wisdom and compassion, they emerge from his back.
From his two shoulders emerge countless hundreds of thousands of billions of yakṣa and rākṣasa kings, because his two shoulders are the locus of great sovereign mastery over power and function.
Because the yakṣa and rākṣasa kings who emerge from it are all able to fly through the air and possess mastery over their powers, this signifies the meaning of protection.
It clarifies that the Bodhisattva manifests great majestic power to guard monasteries and virtuous people.

From his abdomen emerge countless hundreds of thousands of billions of *kiṃnara* kings and their consorts. This clarifies that the abdomen signifies the meaning of "containing"; it clarifies that the *kiṃnara* king is a deity of song and music; and the consorts represent compassion. Thus, he is like a Bodhisattva who, possessing great wisdom and great compassion, contains all virtues within him, and constantly delights sentient beings throughout the ten directions among humans, devas, and the six realms with various Dharma-musics, causing them to be free from all suffering, grief, and affliction.
This is represented by the Kinnara King and his daughter; "King" signifies the meaning of sovereignty.
From within his belly emerge countless Gandharvas and their daughters; these are the deities of music.
This musician dwells on Mount Daśaratna; whenever the devas require music, he goes to those celestial realms to provide musical entertainment.

This also symbolizes that the Bodhisattva’s wisdom and compassion encompass all virtues, using the joy of the Dharma to delight sentient beings, causing them to attain happiness and be freed from all suffering and affliction.

Regarding the emergence of countless hundreds of thousands of billions of wheel-turning kings from their facial gates: the mouth is the gateway through which the true teaching is proclaimed. These Bodhisattvas constantly employ the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence as their fourfold army and the seven factors of enlightenment as their seven treasures. By refraining from meaningless or frivolous speech, they manifest the emergence of wheel-turning kings from their mouths, such that all sounds and voices become the Dharma-teaching.
From his two eyes, countless hundreds of thousands of solar discs emerged, universally illuminating all the great hells and various evil realms.
"Eyes" (*mù*) refers to the eyes themselves; it is because the pupils within the eyes are luminous that they are so called.

This represents how a Bodhisattva constantly observes all sentient beings with the eye of wisdom and the eye of great compassion, establishing teachings according to their faculties to cause them to leave behind all evils.

Regarding the emergence from within the mark of the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa) of countless hundreds of thousands of billions of bodies of Śakra: "Śakra" is here translated as "Capable Master," because he is able to act as the master for all the devas.
The bright hair-treasure between the eyebrows is the place from which all Buddhas emit the light of the fruit of the perfection of the wisdom and compassion of the Middle Way.

By taking Śakra as the presiding lord, it symbolizes that the Bodhisattva, through the practice of the perfection of the wisdom and compassion of the Middle Way, leads and guides all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

From his head emerge a multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms within immeasurable buddha-fields. As for the "head," it signifies the exhaustion of all marks; because his wisdom, compassion, and conduct are perfected and thus infinite, they are measured by the number of atoms in immeasurable buddha-fields.

Regarding "countless hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas emerge from the crown": because the crown is the most honored, exalted, and supreme, the assembly of Buddhas emerges from it; this represents the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
The following twelve locations of transformative function all arise from the crown of the head; thus, there are thirteen locations in total above the crown.
At this stage, the Abiding in the True Mind has already been clarified: it is free from inhalation and exhalation, and its quiescence and function are unimpeded.

Upon reaching the sixth stage among the ten stages (*bhūmi*), it is again identical to this position in that one attains the supernatural power of quiescence (*śānti-ṛddhi*); however, they differ in that the former possesses profound and vast wisdom and compassion, which is symbolized by the Night Goddess (*Rātridevatā*) of the tenth stage, whereas this position is symbolized by a *bhikṣu*.
This can be seen through reflection.
That Sudhana stood still, contemplating and observing for one day and one night, was because his mind of relinquishment through the *dānapāramitā* was perfected.
Seven days and seven nights signify the perfection of the sevenfold precepts.
A half-month signifies the perfection of patience (*kṣānti*);
because patience benefits oneself but does not benefit others, it is designated as a half-month.
The "one month" refers to the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), taking the benefit of oneself and others as that month.
The "six months" refer to the completion of the practice of deliverance (*nairyāṇika-caryā*).
The "six days" refer to the fulfillment of the six kinds of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja said: "This samādhi is called 'Universal Eye’s Relinquishing and Attaining' because the wisdom-eye is like space, universally illuminating the ten directions.

Since the wisdom of emptiness has no substance and all things are likewise fundamentally non-existent, the faculties and their objects are eternally empty; its illumination penetrates everywhere without exception, and it remains unstained by objects—thus it is named 'Universal Eye’s Relinquishing and Attaining.'"

Since there is neither grasping nor rejecting, right view manifests before one; therefore, by virtue of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it is also called the "Pure Light of the Realm of Prajñāpāramitā."

It is also called the "Gate of Universal Adornment and Purity. By employing the wisdom that realizes emptiness, one magically produces various bodies from thirteen locations on the limbs of the body; these emanations arise like clouds, filling the realms of all Buddhas and the worlds of sentient beings throughout the ten directions. They accomplish the work of teaching, transforming, and adorning all sentient beings, yet their body and mind remain entirely free of conceptual thought or perception.
This is the wondrous spirit of non-action that transcends the limits of ordinary cognition; its nature is identical to empty space, and its great function is sovereign.
From the point where I first attained this light of the samādhi of the single Prajñāpāramitā upward, this has been the progressive advancement through the realization of virtues.
These aforementioned six pāramitās fulfill the supramundane mind and complete the practice within the mundane world.

Subsequently, the laywoman Śreṣṭhī (Huishu) manifests the accomplishment of great loving-kindness and great compassion; through the pāramitā of skillful means, she enters into birth and death, adopts the eighty-four thousand *nayuta* patterns of affliction of sentient beings, and gathers in beings through "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*). This refers to her final stage.
As detailed in the subsequent text:
if it were not thus, one would be excessively inclined toward world-transcending liberation and would fail to fulfill great compassion.

From the initial stage of *prathamacittotpādavihāra* on Mount Sumeru, through the *caryāpratipattiviḥāra* in the kingdom of Samudramukha, the *adhimukticaryāviḥāra* on the seashore, from the householder Megha in the kingdom of Darbhasthala to the *gotravihāra*, up to the *śrāvakavihāra* in the forest village, the *samyaktvanyāmāvakrāntiviḥāra*, and the sixth, the *samyakcittavihāra*—this concludes the first cycle of liberation.
From the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression, one accomplishes the subsequent three stages up to the Stage of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).

If these stages were not thus mutually accomplished, the practitioner might attain a single dharma and, claiming it sufficient, fail to know the path of progress; they would then consider what is unattained as attained and what is incomplete as complete.

For this reason, the Dharma-gates of the five stages and their similarities and differences, the wisdom of understanding and practice versus the wisdom of realization, great compassion and various arts, and the universal application of spiritual powers are established, so that one may know them without error and proceed without stagnation, attaining perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta.

By means of this perfect enlightenment, one employs it to subdue habitual tendencies; through the wondrous functions of virtue and all various arts, the path of Samantabhadra is instantaneously accomplished.

Within the wisdom that is without beginning or end and transcends the three periods of time—past, present, and future—one thereby fully realizes all virtues, causing perfect enlightenment to become perfectly luminous and fulfilling the ocean-like conduct of Samantabhadra.
To take the principle of non-action as the Buddha while remaining ignorant of all phenomena is the path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it is not the way of a Buddha.

The seventh stage is the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avivartika-bhūmi*). Here, the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine perfections serve as its companions.

From here, one proceeds southward; by means of clear insight, following the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, one enters into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) through the light of supramundane wisdom within the world. One acts in common with all sentient beings across the eighty-four thousand *nayuta* realms of affliction, employing skillful means—namely, the four methods of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*)—to guide them according to the occasion and lead them to liberation.
The meaning of "Namo" (Homage) is as explained previously.
There is a dwelling place named Sea Tide, which elucidates the seventh practice of skillful means.

By means of the sun of right wisdom, one enters the ocean of birth and death to universally illuminate the eighty-four thousand *nayuta* waves of affliction of all sentient beings, guiding and receiving them all according to their respective capacities, whether great or small.
The dwelling place is named Sea Tide, which clarifies that the Bodhisattva knows the faculties and the timing of sentient beings in order to deliver them, never missing the opportune moment.

There is a grove named Universal Adornment, which clarifies the practice of skillful means; dwelling within the ocean of birth and death and roaming therein, one takes the joy of sentient beings as one's own joy, and for this reason it is called a "grove."

By means of eighty-four thousand nayutas of boundless practices that pervade the minds of all sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to rejoice, resolve upon bodhicitta, and attain the happiness of gods and humans, it is named "Universal Adornment."
In the garden there was an upāsikā named Śūṣa, which in this language means "Fulfilling Wishes.

Because she is able to fulfill all the virtuous vows practiced by sentient beings and bring their wholesome dharmas to completion, she constantly transforms those within the cycle of birth and death without ever ceasing.
She is also called "Intention" (Āśaya), because she fulfills the intentions of all sentient beings and causes them to dedicate all their wholesome dharmas [toward awakening].

The walls, jewel trees, guest halls, and multi-storied pavilions where this laywoman dwells are each said to number one million, as extensively described in the sutra; they cannot be fully recounted here.

All these are due to the profound and vast great compassion of the upāsikās; their environmental rewards and adornments are the fruits that have come without fail, all arising from their past conduct.
By observing the fruit, one knows the cause; since cause and effect correspond, one thereby understands what was practiced.

As the primary retribution for his existence, his body was golden in color and radiant; his dark blue hair hung down over his temples. He wore a crown of sea-treasury pearl nets and was adorned with pure gold armlets from which all the devas emerged. He had earrings made of lion-mouthed *maṇi* jewels and necklaces made of the sovereign *maṇi-rāja* that grants all wishes. Nets of every kind of jewel draped over and covered his body as he sat upon a throne of pure gold.
This clarifies the karmic fruition of the body as a condition.

There are eighty-four thousand nayutas of fellow-practitioner retinues who constantly dwell in this garden; they manifest the practices of great kindness and great compassion, and within each individual practice there are eighty-four thousand nayutas of practice-gates, because they universally encompass all sentient beings.
All environments and physical bodies arise from the karma of the practice of a compassionate mind.
Sudhana asked the upāsikā how long it had been since she first resolved her mind on enlightenment.
Briefly stated, there are as many as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, as detailed in the full text of the sutra.

It is said that he purified his Brahma-conduct in the presence of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers; this has been known by the wisdom of past Buddhas. This clarifies that the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha previously possessed the wisdom of the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*). Taking the six *pāramitās* as the number six, he used the wisdom of the three gates of liberation to illuminate and shatter the afflictions of the six sense organs and six sense objects, thereby accomplishing the light of wisdom of all Buddhas.

Thus, from the three emptinesses, the six perfections, and the seven factors of enlightenment—these thirty-seven auxiliaries of the path—as well as the four means of attraction and the four immeasurable minds, up until the fulfillment of the ten stages and the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, one accomplishes the conduct of Samantabhadra; only when this is spontaneously perfected does one rest.

By means of wisdom that is without merit, compassion is applied without ceasing; through the practice of the six pāramitās, one cultivates a mind largely oriented toward transcendence, reaching the wisdom of the three emptinesses, which constitutes the ultimate path of world-transcendence.

Although he had previously possessed compassion and taught and transformed sentient beings, because his wisdom regarding emptiness was not yet clear, his illumination of all things remained incomplete, and he constantly delighted in the path of world-transcendence.

Upon reaching the sixth stage before him, the bhikṣu Samudrareṇu abides in the "Abiding of the Upright Mind. Having completed his cultivation of the function of illumination, he is detached from inhalation and exhalation; his spiritual wisdom gives rise to transformations with sovereign ease, as has already been clarified above.

With the wondrous wisdom of the three emptinesses, they enter into birth and death to accomplish the practice of great compassion; they accord with the eighty-four thousand unspeakable gates of affliction shared by all sentient beings, acting in concert with them to achieve the stage of consecration.
The first three stages have already been established to bring about the perfection of wisdom and compassion; the subsequent stages will follow in their proper order.

If it were not so, then upon reaching the sixth stage, the Abode of Right Mindfulness (*samyak-citta-vihāra*), one would achieve the accomplishment of mundane and supramundane wisdom. Should there be no subsequent seventh stage, one would immediately re-enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and the practice of great kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*) would be severed. Consequently, the great function within the final three stages could not be realized. For this reason, one arrives at this seventh stage, the Abode of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika-vihāra*).
The Upāsikā Pūrṇamanorathā said:
"Since first giving rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, I have passed through thirty-six Ganges-sands of Buddhas, purely cultivating the Brahma-faring.

She first cited the names of ten ancient Buddhas, such as Dīpaṃkara, and then merely mentioned the number of thirty-six Ganges-sands of Buddhas to represent the liberation of the wisdom of the three emptinesses.
The Buddhas of the three periods and all times past and present are identical; therefore, they are mentioned first.

By means of the Dharma-gates obtained through the wisdom of these three kinds of emptiness and the six *pāramitās*, one enters the sea of birth and death to accomplish the final three stages, thereby perfecting wisdom and accomplishing the practice-gate of Samantabhadra.
The preceding stage is represented by this bhikṣu, while this present stage is represented by the upāsikā, in order to capture the meaning of a portion of worldly compassion.
This is precisely to clarify that for practitioners, both men and women are alike; they must possess compassion, gentleness, and virtuous forbearance, and must not abandon sentient beings.
The teachings of the Sage are subtle and profound; words cannot reach them. Thus, the figures of the bhikṣus, laymen, elders, sons, and daughters are raised as their representations.
One contemplates the image to grasp the meaning; once the meaning is grasped, the image vanishes.
The three emptinesses are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

From these three emptinesses, one instead gives rise to great vows, entering the ten directions, the triple world, and the six realms of existence, vowing to deliver all sentient beings until they are exhausted; as long as sentient beings are not yet exhausted, the practices of Samantabhadra shall never cease.
The same applies to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Through the vows and practices of the seventh stage, one accomplishes the subsequent eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, as well as the conduct of Samantabhadra.
The Great Function and Divine Power of the Tathāgata accomplish the activities of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth: if one does not give rise to great vows in the seventh bhūmi to enter the cycle of birth and death, but merely practices the pāramitās up to the sixth bhūmi and attains the supramundane transcendental powers of quiescence, one will consider oneself satisfied. One would thus fail to realize that what has been practiced is but the excellence of the subsequent seventh, eighth, and ninth bhūmis, and that the constant practice of Samantabhadra following the fruit of Buddhahood would be severed.
The principles within these ten stages are similar to those [of the ten bhūmis], with wisdom and compassion increasing and expanding, though they differ in the ripening of their habitual practices.
Within these ten abodes, the bhikṣu, householder, elder, upāsikā, rishi, brahmin, king, and princess serve as the analogies for the ten bhūmis.

With nine night deities and one wife of the Tathāgata, Gopā, the long night of birth and death is shattered; through these divine manifestations, the relative superiority or inferiority of their meritorious practices may be understood.
Sudhana asked, "Noble One!
How long will it be before you attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The upāsikā replied: “My vow shall not end until I have brought even a single sentient being to maturity, up to and including the point when I have brought all sentient beings to maturity.”
"When the offerings to all Buddhas are exhausted, and the adornment of all places of enlightenment is exhausted, my vows shall likewise be exhausted.
This intention clarifies that the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi have no beginning or end, and that the practices of Samantabhadra have no beginning or end.
From the passage "Since I have only known this liberation-gate of the banner of sorrowless peace" onwards, it concerns the advancement through the cultivation of virtues.
This clarifies that those in this stage enter the ocean of birth and death, achieve great compassion, do not weary of clamor and bustle, and possess minds free from affliction.
Even if immeasurable sentient beings were to afflict them all at once, they would remain constantly joyful; therefore, it is called the liberation of the Banner of Peaceful Security Free from Sorrow.
The eighth stage, the Abode of Youthfulness (*kumārabhūmi*), takes the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) as its primary quality, with the other nine as its companions.

In this southern region, at the place of the ocean tide, there is a land named Nalasu, which in this language means "Not Lazy. This signifies that the Bodhisattvas at this stage have attained an increase in a portion of effortlessness-wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*); they recollect their original vows and give rise to compassionate conduct, practicing without indolence, which is twice as superior as before; therefore, it is called "Not Lazy."

Regarding the designation "Ocean Tide" for this same stage: the preceding stage was that of nurturing great compassion; in this stage, wisdom increases and becomes luminous, such that wisdom and compassion are realized as a single essence.
Because one dwells in this seventh stage, wisdom arises from compassion; in the tenth stage, the Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣeka*), compassion is practiced through wisdom.
The daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja was named Maitrāyaṇī;
there was also a seer named Vemacitra, which in this language means "One Whose Voice Is Terrifying."
In the eighth stage, the Youthful (Kumārabhūmi), a portion of right knowledge increases and becomes luminous; the sounds and voices he utters cause all those who are heterodox to tremble with fear.
For what reason is this stage symbolized by a *ṛṣi* (sage)?
There are two meanings:
first, because their wisdom is as pure as that of a seer, they are free from the five desires;
second, it clarifies that having attained the increase of wisdom, they are able to follow along with those of false views to assist them in the process of rebirth.
It guides those who seek immortality, causing them to enter into right gnosis.
As for the immortal’s stroking of Sudhana’s crown, it signifies that he has been granted permission and confirmation by means of the seal of trust, reaching this stage of gnosis without doubt.

As Sudhana’s hand was grasped by the Vidyā-mantra to guide him, he immediately saw his own body traveling to worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields in the ten directions, arriving at the abodes of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, and beholding those buddha-fields along with their assemblies.
As explained at length in the sutras:
because one enters the stage of wisdom with clarity and increases that clarity, one is able to see and teach as the Buddha does.
One attains mastery over the buddha-fields, the body, and the objective realm; for wisdom is like space, seeing the Buddha and his environment as pervasive throughout space without exception.
Within a single thought-moment, by the power of samādhi, he sealed immeasurable kalpas so that they were all seen simultaneously.
The rishi released Sudhana’s hand, and it returned to its former state.
This is the stage of Youthful Innocence (*kumārabhūmi*).

Having first reached a portion of the level of wisdom with increased clarity, one is able to perceive the realms of the various Buddha-lands only through the guidance and empowerment provided by the noble ones.
When one reaches the ultimate fulfillment of the Buddha’s merit, the ten directions are always manifest before one, requiring no further exertion of effort.

From the point where it says, "From me, having known this Bodhisattva's Liberation of the Unsurpassed Banner," onwards, this is the section on the advancement of virtue through the recommendation of others.
The ninth stage, the Abode of the Dharma Prince, has the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) as its primary quality, with the remaining nine as its companions.
Regarding "in this southern direction," it refers to proceeding from the previously ascended entry into the subsequent position.
The meaning of "namo" (homage) is as previously explained.
There is a village named Īśāna, which means "Long and Straight"; by virtue of this rank of Dharma Prince and Dharma Master, one's wisdom becomes long and straight.
Because they preach the teachings to benefit sentient beings, they have grown beyond their previous stage; because they rely on faculties that are not crooked, they are said to be "long and straight.
This collectively clarifies that there is nothing within the mind or its objects that is not the Dharma-realm, which is termed a "village."

There was a brahmin named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa; because he had attained a wisdom that accorded with heterodoxy, he subjected his body to the five heats without being harmed, and thus he was named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
The fire of the world arises from afflictions; wisdom is cool and superior to afflictions, and because it surpasses afflictions, even fire cannot burn it.
This wisdom enters the realm of divine function; it is not something produced by the traces of the mind.

One ascends a mountain of blades and enters a mass of fire, where firewood is piled on all four sides like mountains and flames reach the heavens. The mountain of blades is steep and lofty; one casts oneself into the midst of the fire to manifest that through cultivation one has reached this stage, wherein afflictions and karma have perished.
With such wisdom, he was able to shatter all false views and lead others to the right view.
He exhorted Sudhana to ascend a mountain of blades; when Sudhana harbored doubts, the devas offered consolation and encouragement, causing him to be free from doubt.
By means of the radiance of the Vajrajvālā-samādhi, one burns the fuel of afflictions and severs the net of false views, causing beings to return to the True Dharma.
For those who enter this internal Vajra-samādhi, afflictions are entirely extinguished, like a pool of cool clarity.

Within the dharma manifested by the mind, taking the wisdom of signlessness as the mountain of blades and the wondrous light of essencelessness as that which can shatter delusions constitutes the Vajra-Flame Samādhi.
If one were to maintain a state of blazing, radiant vajra-forms, it would be impossible to destroy the dust of conceptual attachment and clinging.

The Master of the Treatise states in verse: "The fire of fundamental wisdom pervades all of space; it gives rise to the adamantine blade of sublime prajñā-wisdom, which can shatter the stubborn karma of sentient beings and restore them to the wondrous radiance of fundamental wisdom."
When the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) manifests as ignorance, it is revealed through the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*) from the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Now, having reached this ninth stage of the Dharma King within the ten stages, one gives rise to function from the fundamental wisdom; this wondrous wisdom benefits sentient beings, and thus constitutes the fire of the Vajra-samādhi.

He raises the mountain of the sword of immeasurable wisdom to illuminate and sever the afflictions of all sentient beings throughout the long night, and through skillful means, he guides and receives those who engage in deluded practices and asceticism, such as the five fires that scorch the body.
The tenth stage, the Abode of Empowerment (Abhiṣeka-vihāra), has the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) as its primary quality, with the other nine as its companions.
To the south there is a city named Siṃhavikrīḍita, which clarifies the perfection of wisdom within the Abode of Empowerment.

In this stage, one practices compassion through wisdom while dwelling within the ocean of birth and death; realizing that the fundamental essence of the mind-ground is without arising or ceasing, one does not fear birth and death, and is thus named the Lion Banner King (*Siṃhadhvaja-rāja*).

Within a single wisdom, he simultaneously manifests physical bodies before all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, responding universally like an echo; he pervades everywhere at once, just as a lion, in a single moment, causes his entire body to shake with vigorous power.
There was a maiden named Maitrāyaṇī, the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja.
King Siṃhadhvaja was wisdom, while the maiden Maitrāyaṇī was the practice of loving-kindness and compassion.
This stage clarifies that one proceeds from wisdom to practice compassion and acts in concert with the world.
Because there is no defiled habituation, this is symbolized by a young girl.
For example, the seventh [stage], the laywoman Śreṣṭhidārīkā, proceeds from compassion to achieve wisdom; because she still retains defiled habituation, she is symbolized by a laywoman.
All these figures represent the knowledge of the Dharma; once the Dharma is attained, the figures vanish—this can be seen through contemplation.
The five hundred young maidens who serve as attendants represent the afflictions within the five aggregates.
The Sūtra states: "Upon a single aggregate (skandha) there are five hundred afflictions; upon the five aggregates there are two thousand five hundred afflictions.

By means of this practice of wisdom and compassion, one universally gathers the five hundred practices of the pāramitās across the five stages, and aligns one's own conduct with the five hundred afflictions of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
There were as many as eighty-four thousand [deities], with five hundred serving as leaders.

They resided in the Vairocana-garbha Hall; taking the clarity of great compassion as their abiding place within the treasury of fundamental wisdom’s radiance, they formed the very substance of the hall.

As for the one who preaches the sublime Dharma from a seat adorned with celestial robes, a network of gold-threaded sandalwood, and nāga-victory banners, he does so by giving rise to wondrous wisdom from the fundamental gnosis of the Lion Banner King.
By means of the dragon, a great rain of Dharma is brought down to moisten and benefit sentient beings.

*Candana* is the name of a fragrance; because this incense can pacify the feverish afflictions of venomous snakes, when the heat is intense and the afflictions of poison are rampant, one wraps oneself with it from the tree, and the feverish afflictions become cool and refreshing.
This clarifies that when this virtuous friend lets fall the rain of Dharma, the venomous snakes of ignorance all attain coolness.
Regarding the seat of the golden thread net-garment: "thread" has the meaning of piercing through; "net" refers to the net of the teachings; and "garment" has the meaning of covering.
Because you are skillfully able to penetrate the net of the teachings and provide protection for all sentient beings, you have earned your place upon this seat.
As for Sudhana’s journey to the palace gate to seek that woman, it is the Palace of Compassion belonging to King Jñāna where she is to be sought.
Contemplating their retributive fruits, within each and every realm there are all Tathāgatas.

From the initial generation of the bodhicitta, through the attainment of enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the manifestation of entry into nirvana, they interpenetrate one another like the reflections in a net of Indra.
"By means of this seal of the *pāramitās*, one seals the karma of the three periods of time— past, present, and future— and thus all objective realms are completely exhausted.
The maiden said to Sudhana,
"O son of good family!..."
"This is the gate of the universal adornment of the *pāramitās*.

I sought and obtained this dharma-gate from as many Buddhas as there are sands in thirty-six Ganges Rivers. This means that the wisdom of the three emptinesses and the six perfections constitute the number of Buddhas; what was expounded by one Buddha was not repeated by the others.
By means of clarity, one proceeds from fundamental wisdom to give rise to the wisdom of the three gates of liberation; these are all the wisdom of the Buddha.
This is also a single set of the three gates of liberation: the wisdom of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The practice-gate of the six perfections transforms the internal and external objects of the six sense-faculties of all sentient beings, making them entirely pure.
It is universally able to adorn the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, making them all the wisdom of the Buddha, as explained in the following text.

The immeasurable *prajñāpāramitā* takes as its essence the arising of the wisdom of the three empties through fundamental gnosis; it is able to purify all the various karmic gates of sentient beings and cause them to achieve the wisdom of the Tathāgata, all of which take the wisdom of the three empties as their essence, as explained extensively in the sutras.
From the passage beginning with "Since I have known only this Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā" onwards, there is an advancement through the promotion of virtues.

This clarifies that in the seventh stage, one enters the ocean of birth and death and acts in concert with all sentient beings regarding the eighty-four thousand afflictions and the unspeakably numerous afflictions that are as vast as space, practicing alongside them in every way.
Upon reaching this tenth stage of abiding, the practice of cultivation is fulfilled and the course of wisdom reaches its completion.
Returning once more from fundamental wisdom, one gives rise to eighty-four thousand unspeakable forms of wisdom.
The fundamental wisdom arises as a whole, taking the three emptinesses as its essence; it is capable of destroying all afflictions within the six sense organs of all sentient beings.
Therefore, if there were not the manifold afflictions of sentient beings, the wisdom of the three emptinesses would likewise not exist.
The afflictions of sentient beings are vast and manifold; the Prajñāpāramitā is vast and manifold; and the emanations of the Tathāgata are likewise vast and manifold.

By employing the functions of the merit, wisdom, and spiritual transformations cultivated during the Ten Abodes, one accomplishes all the practice-gates for benefiting sentient beings within the Ten Practices, as well as the obstacle of the lack of mastery over one's own habitual tendencies and conduct, thereby rendering them free and unimpeded.

After the ten spiritual friends mentioned above, ordinary persons practice both the mundane and the supramundane; in the supramundane, there is a predominance of the wisdom of emptiness and liberation, as well as a supramundane mind of great compassion.

Regarding the gates of arts, governance, transformation, and benefit for sentient beings that have not yet been studied, one establishes positions and clarifies the teachings; thus, the five stages are distinguished by their anteriority and posteriority.

However, for one who practices them, nothing is excluded from a single moment, a single dharma, or a single position, as they universally encompass all prior and subsequent times and dharmas; for within the realm of wisdom, there is neither past nor present.
